extracted.intended_audience: The people (voters) of the State of New York / general public deciding on ratification (late-18th century)
extracted.subtask_description: An 18th-century persuasive political essay arguing for ratification of the proposed U.S. Constitution and explaining why adoption now — with later amendment if needed — is preferable to delaying for perfection. It addresses practical, fiscal, institutional, and moral considerations aimed at voters and civic actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of the proposed government
rubrics_metrics.description: The sources of additional expense from the establishment of the proposed Constitution are much fewer than may have been imagined; they are counterbalanced by considerable objects of saving; and while it is questionable on which side the scale will preponderate, it is certain that a government less expensive would be incompetent to the purposes of the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Savings arise from reduced congressional session time, transfer of many functions to the President, and decreased demands on State legislatures. Any extra expense (e.g., support of judges) is modest under reasonable plans. The test is net effect: additional expenses must be weighed against clear savings from structural changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation of routine national business to the Executive
rubrics_metrics.description: A great part of the business which now keeps Congress sitting through the year will be transacted by the President... Even the management of foreign negotiations will naturally devolve upon him, according to general principles concerted with the Senate, and subject to their final concurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the Constitution's allocation of administrative and diplomatic functions to the Executive will reduce legislative workload and permit shorter legislative sessions, with the Senate retaining final concurrence on key matters (treaties, appointments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction in State legislature burden and consequent savings
rubrics_metrics.description: The sessions of the State legislatures have been protracted greatly beyond what was necessary for the execution of the mere local business of the States because they have had to provide for requisitions of the United States. The new system will do in the first instance what has been done by two thousand and upwards, probably by sixty-five persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess anticipated reduction in time and costs for State legislatures once national business is centralized; quantify comparative numbers (current many vs proposed small federal body) and account for that as an offset to federal expenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of the Union as a restraint on local factions and ambitious individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: The additional securities to republican government, to liberty and to property, to be derived from the adoption of the plan consist chiefly in the restraints which the preservation of the Union will impose on local factions and insurrections, and on the ambition of powerful individuals in single States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the Constitution by its capacity to reduce internal factionalism and to prevent emergence of state-level despots by creating national constraints on local abuses of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diminution of opportunities for foreign intrigue
rubrics_metrics.description: The adoption will diminish the opportunities to foreign intrigue, which the dissolution of the Confederacy would invite and facilitate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how a stronger Union reduces the ability of foreign powers to exploit divisions among states; weigh this foreign-policy stabilizing effect in evaluating the plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention of extensive military establishments arising from interstate wars
rubrics_metrics.description: The adoption will prevent extensive military establishments, which could not fail to grow out of wars between the States in a disunited situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a unified government reduces the risk of interstate conflict and the consequent growth of standing militaries that threaten liberty and public resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express guaranty of a republican form of government for each state
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the securities consists in the express guaranty of a republican form of government to each [state].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the value of a constitutional guarantee that preserves republican forms across all states as a protection for citizens' liberties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute exclusion of titles of nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: One security is the absolute and universal exclusion of titles of nobility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the prohibition of hereditary honors as a republican safeguard; include it among checks protecting equality and preventing aristocratic concentrations of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precautions against state practices undermining property, credit, and morals
rubrics_metrics.description: The precautions against the repetition of those practices on the part of the State governments which have undermined the foundations of property and credit, have planted mutual distrust... and have occasioned an almost universal prostration of morals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine constitutional provisions that limit state abuses undermining property and credit; consider their likely effectiveness in restoring confidence and economic order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative ease of subsequent amendments versus original adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: It is susceptible of absolute demonstration, that it will be far more easy to obtain subsequent than previous amendments to the Constitution... To its complete establishment throughout the Union, [a revised plan] will therefore require the concurrence of thirteen States. If, on the contrary, the Constitution proposed should once be ratified by all the States as it stands, alterations in it may at any time be effected by nine States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the numerical mechanics (adoption vs amendment thresholds) as a decision metric: initial ratification of the proposed Constitution makes future targeted amendments more feasible than attempting to adopt a wholly new plan now.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicality of obtaining amendments post-adoption (Article V obligation)
rubrics_metrics.description: By the fifth article of the plan, the Congress will be obliged 'on the application of the legislatures of two thirds of the States... to call a convention for proposing amendments'... The Congress 'shall call a convention.' Nothing in this particular is left to the discretion of that body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor in Article V's mandatory procedure as an institutional guarantee that amendments, when sufficiently supported by states, will be deliberated and proposed; this reduces the concern that national rulers could block desirable changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid seeking perfection before adoption; rely on experience and time
rubrics_metrics.description: To balance a large state or society on general laws is a work of so great difficulty... EXPERIENCE must guide their labor; TIME must bring it to perfection, and the FEELING of inconveniences must correct the mistakes which they inevitably fall into in their first trials and experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer adoption of a workable, though imperfect, constitutional framework now, with the expectation that shortfalls will be identified and corrected through experience and subsequent amendment rather than risking instability by delaying adoption for an unattainable perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public duty and virtue in deciding on the Constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man is bound to answer these questions to himself, according to the best of his conscience and understanding... No partial motive, no particular interest, no pride of opinion, no temporary passion or prejudice, will justify... an improper election of the part he is to act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voters and decision-makers should weigh the question soberly, avoiding factionalism, personal interest, and prejudice; decisions should be guided by conscience and judgment rather than party zeal or private advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency in critique (avoid hypocritical objections)
rubrics_metrics.description: The resemblance of the plan of the convention to the act which organizes the government of this State holds, not less with regard to many of the supposed defects, than to the real excellences of the former... a man must have slender pretensions to consistency, who can rail at the latter for imperfections which he finds no difficulty in excusing in the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should be judged for consistency: objections to the national plan that mirror defects in existing state constitutions are not persuasive; evaluate criticisms by whether they apply equally to familiar accepted institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of necessary compromise among diverse parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The compacts which are to embrace thirteen distinct States in a common bond of amity and union, must as necessarily be a compromise of as many dissimilar interests and inclinations. How can perfection spring from such materials?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that a constitution for many states must reconcile divergent interests; treat the presence of compromises not as fatal defects but as inevitable features enabling union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk assessment: dangers of remaining without a national government
rubrics_metrics.description: A NATION, without a NATIONAL GOVERNMENT, is, in my view, an awful spectacle... I can reconcile it to no rules of prudence to let go the hold we now have... and recommence the course. I dread... POWERFUL INDIVIDUALS... are enemies to a general national government in every possible shape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether to adopt the Constitution, weigh the tangible risks of continued disunion — anarchy, civil war, foreign exploitation, and the rise of demagogic/ military despotism — against the imperfections of the proposed plan.
